newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Euro stocks end on high note, Paris recovers.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Euro stocks end on high note, Paris recovers.

text.p: European bourses shrugged off a poor start on Wall Street to close with solid gains on Tuesday as Paris recovered its nerve despite the strong showing of the Left in parliamentary elections.
In foreign exchanges, the dollar climbed by over a pfennig in late trade, supported by renewed prospect of higher U.S. interest rates after robust U.S. consumer confidence data.
It was also helped by the mark slipping against other European currencies as the French poll increased expectations of a softer European single currency.
Most attention was fixed on equities after 10 European bourses, including Frankfurt and Zurich, scored trading peaks on Monday, encouraged by a big rally in Wall Street at its last session on Friday.

Paris, which stood out on Monday by plunging four percent after the surprise first round advance by left-wing parties in the National Assembly polls, rebounded to close up nearly one percent at 2680.34 points on the CAC-40 index.

Investors had clearly recovered their nerve, betting that even if the left won next Sunday's runoff legislative election, there would be no radical change in economic policy. The franc also firmed and bond prices were steady.

Analysts said they did not believe Prime Minister Alain Juppe's surprise decision to resign would boost the centre-right's chances in next Sunday's final vote, saying it smacked too much of panic in the ruling coalition's ranks.
But, said one share analyst, "People just figure even if it is the left in power, they will have to follow the discipline imposed by world financial markets."

Shares in defence electronics firm Thomson-CSF rallied 2.22 percent to 175.10 francs after falling on Monday amid fears its privatisation could be scrapped by a Socialist administration. Other privatisation stocks also recovered, such as bank Credit Lyonnais, which jumped 5.83 percent to 225.10 francs.

"There were fears the privatisation programme would have to be stopped but there is a growing realisation a Socialist-led government will also have to sell shares," a trader said. "They will need it for their budget.
In Frankfurt, floor trade extended its bull run to end at another record close of 3,674.36 points, eclipsing Monday's peak, but volumes were thin.
In after-hours electronic trade, the market ran out of steam and slipped into the minus column in mid-afternoon trade.
Dealers said the rally petered out mainly because of the absence of new data to drive the market past the psychologically key 3,700 point level.

London, which was closed for a public holiday on Monday, ended up 0.4 percent, lifted by a buoyant bank sector but its early enthusiasm was dulled by Wall Street which fell 0.2 percent at its opening.
Bank shares continued to outperform the broad market as institutions, still flush with cash, scrambled to increase their weightings ahead of the Halifax Building Society flotation on June 2.
"We're seeing an unprecedented squeeze," said one trader of the sector's recent performance. "It's being driven by these upcoming flotations."
In currency markets, the dollar was boosted against the mark by the fresh uncertainty over EMU following the French vote and ahead of the next round on Sunday.

"The election results suggest, if repeated next Sunday, that you are likely to get a broader grouping towards EMU, which does suggest that the euro will be a weaker currency," said Jeremy Stretch currency strategist at NatWest Markets.
A softer euro would benefit currencies outside the system such as the dollar and the Swiss franc, analysts said.
The U.S. currency was also helped against the yen by the prospects for higher rates after the strong U.S. consumer confidence figures.
The U.S. Conference Board said its May consumer confidence index hit a 28-year peak to 127.1 against an upwardly revised 118.5 for April and well above analysts' expectations of 114.4.
"This is not normally a key figure for the market but at this stage of the economic cycle, this rise is more significant," said Thomas Rayner, international economist at Societe Generale Strauss
Elsewhere, the beleaguered Czech crown was hit hard after the central bank eliminated the band within which it had moved against a mark/dollar basket.
The crown tumbled on Tuesday, trading at 19.4 against the mark, compared with 18.1 before the central bank made its move.
STOCK PRICES
London's FTSE 100 finished up 19.8 points to 4,681.6.
The Paris CAC-40 index ended at 25.60 points at 2680.34.
Frankfurt's DAX index closed up 16.50 points at 3674.36.
CURRENCIES
The dollar stood at 1.7030 marks and 116.57 yen in late European trading compared with 1.6899 marks and 116.33 yen on Monday.
PRECIOUS METALS
Gold was closed at $343.75 ounce, compared to $343.10 in late trade on Monday. Silver was one cent down at $4.74 in late trade.
